abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive and treatment-resistant brain tumor with poor prognosis despite surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. Sonodynamic therapy (SDT), which combines low-intensity focused ultrasound with systemically or orally administered sonosensitizers, has emerged as a promising non-invasive approach to achieve localized tumor cell killing via reactive oxygen species. Recent advances in nanomedicine have enabled the development of orally absorbable, blood–brain barrier permeable delivery systems that enhance tumor targeting and ultrasound responsiveness. Preclinical studies have demonstrated consistent anti-tumor efficacy and immune activation, while early clinical trials suggest SDT is safe, feasible, and potentially effective in recurrent GBM. This review outlines recent progress in SDT-based strategies for GBM, with emphasis on mechanistic insights, delivery innovations, and clinical translation.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most prevalent and lethal primary malignant brain tumor in adults, accounting for approximately 15% of all intracranial neoplasms and 45%–50% of malignant tumors [1]. The World Health Organization (WHO) calls it a grade IV astrocytoma, and it has a number of histological features that suggest it is aggressive [2]. Microvascular proliferation (MVP) and pseudopalisading necrosis are two of the most important signs of this disease [3]. Hypoxia-driven overexpression of vascular endothelial growth factor causes MVP, which makes blood vessels that are abnormal, leaky, and structurally unstable [4]. At the same time, pseudopalisading necrosis shows ischemic cell death because the tumor grows too quickly for the blood vessels to keep up. The surviving tumor cells form palisade-like structures around the necrotic cells. These pathologic patterns show the metabolic and vascular stress that causes GBM to grow and resist treatment [5].

The WHO classification of central nervous system tumors goes beyond histological criteria and includes molecular profiling in the diagnostic framework [6]. GBMs that are isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) wildtype and have one or more of the following changes are considered GBM, no matter how they look under a microscope: telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) promoter mutations, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) amplification, or a combination of gaining chromosome 7 and losing chromosome 10 (+7/−10) [6]. These molecular changes are strongly linked to a bad clinical outcome and are often seen with other changes, such as the loss of phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN), deletions of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A/B (CDKN2A and CDKN2B), and the activation of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) pathways [7].

GBM is further characterized by pronounced heterogeneity and diffuse infiltration, features that enable resistant subclones and residual cells to escape surgical eradication [8,9,10,11]. Glioma stem-like cells (GSCs), a subset of tumor-initiating cells that live in perivascular and hypoxic niches, are an essential part of the GBM microenvironment [12]. GSCs are distinguished by their increased ability to self-renew, multilineage differentiate, and repair DNA, as well as by the expression of stemness markers like CD133, Nestin, and SOX2 [13]. These cells exhibit strong resistance to radiation and alkylating agents like temozolomide (TMZ), and it is thought that they are responsible for both tumor maintenance and post-treatment recurrence [14]. In addition to such cellular mechanisms of resistance, a formidable physical barrier arises from the heterogeneous integrity of the blood–brain barrier (BBB). While the tumor core often develops leaky vasculature due to neo-angiogenesis, the infiltrative margins generally retain an intact BBB, which limits therapeutic penetration [15]. This regional heterogeneity results in subtherapeutic drug levels at sites where residual tumor cells persist, ultimately contributing to treatment failure and disease progression [16,17].

These cellular and structural barriers largely account for the limited efficacy of current multimodal approaches. Despite maximum safe surgical resection, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, median survival remains only 14–16 months, with 5-year survival under 10% [18]. Almost every patient has a tumor recurrence, usually 6–9 months after starting treatment, and second-line options such as bevacizumab, lomustine, or re-irradiation provide only transient benefit [19,20]. Such poor outcomes are primarily driven by inadequate BBB penetration, resistance to alkylating agents like TMZ (especially in tumors with an unmethylated O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase [MGMT] promoter), therapy-resistant GSCs, and the persistence of infiltrative tumor cells, while attempts to intensify treatment are constrained by systemic toxicity and the neurotoxic ceiling of radiotherapy [21,22]. Many patients are ineligible or intolerant of long-term device-based therapies, and although tumor treating fields (TTFields) have modestly improved survival, their use remains limited [23]. The immunologically inert microenvironment of GBM, characterized by low neoantigen expression, has so far blunted the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors and therapeutic vaccines [24]. These current limitations highlight the need for new therapeutic approaches that are non-invasive, able to circumvent or alter the BBB, efficient against diverse treatment-resistant tumor types, and possibly complementary to immunotherapy or conventional treatment. Among the emerging strategies, sonodynamic therapy (SDT) has attracted attention as a promising non-invasive modality capable of overcoming these challenges.

sec.title: SDT AS A NON-INVASIVE, SELECTIVE STRATEGY FOR GBM
sec.p: SDT offers a non-invasive, spatially selective platform for GBM treatment that addresses the limitations of conventional modalities [25]. Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is applied to the tumor site after a sonosensitizer has been administered orally or systemically [25]. Ultrasound is particularly well-suited for deep-seated brain tumors because of its capacity to focus energy with millimeter precision and pass through the skull several centimeters [26]. SDT functions via a non-ionizing, non-thermal mechanism, in contrast to photodynamic therapy (PDT), which permits repeated application without cumulative toxicity. Because of these characteristics, SDT can target the margins of infiltrative tumors while preserving the surrounding brain tissue. SDT platforms can be designed to circumvent the BBB through focused ultrasound or targeted nanomedicine techniques, which are relevant to GBM [27]. Furthermore, preliminary research suggests the possibility of promoting anti-tumor immunity as well as preferential cytotoxicity against GSCs.

sec.title: Mechanistic basis and therapeutic rationale of SDT in GBM
sec.p: Focused ultrasound combined with a sonosensitizer triggers a sequence of biophysical and biochemical reactions that result in the therapeutic action of SDT [28]. Oscillating pressure waves interact with gas-filled microbubbles or naturally occurring cavitation nuclei in the tumor microenvironment when exposed to ultrasound [29]. This causes either inertial cavitation (violent collapse) or stable cavitation (continuous oscillation), the latter of which creates confined high-temperature, high-pressure zones that can have sonochemical effects [29]. The pyrolysis of nearby molecules brought on by these effects produces extremely reactive free radicals, such as singlet oxygen and hydroxyl radicals.

Numerous sonosensitizers absorb the mechanical or sonochemical energy released by cavitation and change into an excited state; these are typically derivatives of porphyrin, phthalocyanine, or xanthene or constructs based on nanoparticles [30]. Cytotoxic reactive oxygen specie (ROS) like singlet oxygen and superoxide can be produced by these excited sensitizer molecules, transferring energy to molecular oxygen [31]. The produced ROS ultimately result in necrotic or apoptotic cell death by oxidatively damaging nuclear DNA, mitochondrial proteins, and cellular membranes. Spatial selectivity is made possible by this highly localized process, which minimizes systemic toxicity by keeping the sensitizer chemically inert in the absence of ultrasound activation [32]. Furthermore, a process known as sonoporation occurs when the mechanical stress produced during cavitation momentarily increases the permeability of tight junctions and cell membranes. This increases therapeutic agents’ intracellular uptake and could make it easier for drugs to enter tumor areas with inadequate blood flow [33]. Interestingly, ultrasound can also be used to temporarily and permanently open the BBB, especially when paired with circulating microbubbles. In the case of GBM, where intact BBB structures in infiltrative tumor margins severely obstruct drug delivery, this capability is extremely beneficial [34]. These effects, which include membrane permeabilization, BBB modulation, and localized ROS generation, give SDT a distinct mechanistic profile that makes it an excellent choice for treating GBM. Unlike systemic chemotherapy or immunotherapy, which are limited by BBB impermeability and off-target toxicity, SDT offers the ability to spatially restrict cytotoxic activity to the tumor region with millimeter precision. Focused ultrasound can penetrate several centimeters into brain tissue, including through the intact skull, making it feasible to target deep or inoperable lesions [35]. This is important in GBM, where tumor cells often infiltrate surrounding brain parenchyma and evade conventional therapies.

Overall, the mechanistic versatility of SDT, including its capacity to penetrate the skull, localize cytotoxicity, modulate the BBB, target redox-sensitive cells, and stimulate anti-tumor immunity, makes it particularly well-suited for addressing the multifaceted therapeutic challenges of GBM. When combined with nanomedicine-based delivery systems, including orally absorbable formulations capable of systemic distribution and brain accumulation, SDT represents a powerful platform for non-invasive and precision-targeted therapy. In the context of GBM, a disease defined by spatial complexity, resistance, and therapeutic inaccessibility, SDT offers an unprecedented opportunity to overcome these barriers in a clinically translatable manner.

sec.title: Design strategies for orally deliverable sonosensitizers
sec.p: Not only must sonosensitizer chemistry and ultrasound parameters be optimized when designing an effective SDT platform for GBM, but drug delivery logistics must also be carefully considered, particularly when aiming for patient-friendly administration routes like oral delivery [36]. In neuro-oncology, delivering therapeutics across the BBB has long been a challenge. However, oral administration adds another level of complexity because of the harsh gastrointestinal environment, variable absorption, and first-pass metabolism [37]. However, a novel approach to brain tumor treatment would be made possible by an orally absorbable nanomedicine that provides glioma tissue with a sonosensitizer and permits externally controlled activation by ultrasound, possibly opening the door to repeatable, non-invasive, and outpatient-compatible SDT regimens [38].

The clinical application of 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA), a small-molecule pro-sensitizer, given orally to GBM patients for fluorescence-guided resection, served as a proof-of-concept for this paradigm [39]. 5-ALA has been demonstrated to penetrate the BBB and be selectively absorbed by glioma cells, where it was converted into protoporphyrin IX (PpIX), a porphyrin derivative that serves as a photosensitizer and fluorescent marker [40]. Crucially, preclinical research showed that 5-ALA-mediated SDT caused mitochondrial ROS generation and glioma cell apoptosis, and PpIX was also discovered to function as a sonosensitizer [41,42]. A number of early-stage clinical trials have started assessing 5-ALA-enabled SDT in populations of adult and pediatric gliomas, offering fundamental support for a larger class of oral SDT nanomedicines [43].

To expand beyond 5-ALA, researchers are currently developing nanocarrier-based systems that can protect sonosensitizers during gastrointestinal transit, enhance absorption, and enable targeting to the brain [44]. These nanocarriers must address competing physiological constraints: 1) resist gastric degradation, 2) penetrate the intestinal barrier, 3) evade first-pass hepatic metabolism, and 4) cross the BBB to reach glioma tissue. Therefore, biocompatible nanocarriers such as solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs), polymeric nanoparticles (e.g., poly(lactic-co-glycolic) acid [PLGA], chitosan), and PEGylated liposomes have been employed to encapsulate hydrophobic or labile sonosensitizers, thereby improving oral stability and bioavailability [45]. For example, chitosan-coated SLNs were shown to enhance intestinal retention, mucoadhesion, and pH-responsive release, leading to higher systemic exposure of the payload after oral administration in mice models [46]. Once in systemic circulation, the nanomedicine must be optimized to accumulate in brain tumors. Surface modification with targeting ligands, such as transferrin, insulin, or lactoferrin peptides, has been shown to promote receptor-mediated transcytosis across the BBB in preclinical glioma models. By imitating inflammatory leukocyte trafficking, macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles have been shown in more recent studies to evade immune clearance, extend circulation time, and accumulate in orthotopic GBM [47].

Collectively, these studies support the feasibility of developing orally deliverable, ultrasound-triggerable nanomedicines tailored for GBM SDT. Although challenges remain, such as variability in oral absorption, inter-patient differences in gut permeability, and BBB transport efficiency, the integration of nanocarrier engineering with SDT represents a powerful strategy for non-invasive, spatially targeted glioma treatment. In the following section, we examine recent preclinical and clinical studies that have implemented these design principles, highlighting key advances in sonosensitizer development, therapeutic outcomes, and translational progress in GBM.

sec.title: EXPERIMENTAL AND CLINICAL PROGRESS IN GBM SDT
Preclinical evidence of efficacy and mechanism
sec.p: A growing body of preclinical research has demonstrated the efficacy of SDT in GBM models, validating its ability to induce ROS-mediated cytotoxicity, modulate tumor immune responses, and overcome barriers such as the BBB [48]. These studies span a wide range of optimizing sonosensitizers, including organic dyes (e.g., IR-780, Rose Bengal), porphyrins (e.g., chlorin e6, 5-ALA), and inorganic materials such as titanium dioxide and metal-doped carbon nanostructures. Mouse and rat orthotopic glioma models have been the predominant systems, enabling evaluation of intratumoral effects and survival outcomes. Several early studies established proof-of-concept using 5-ALA–mediated SDT in subcutaneous and intracranial tumor-bearing mice. These experiments confirmed that ultrasound-triggered activation of intracellular PpIX leads to caspase-dependent apoptosis and significantly prolongs survival compared to controls. Subsequently, more sophisticated nanomedicine designs have been explored. Titanium dioxide and BaTiO3-based piezoelectric nanoparticles demonstrated enhanced ROS generation and synergy with chemotherapeutic agents such as TMZ. Other efforts focused on integrating immune modulation, such as macrophage-mimetic carriers loaded with checkpoint inhibitors that both ablated tumors and stimulated CD8+ T cell infiltration. sec.title: Clinical translation of SDT in GBM
sec.p: The compelling anti-tumor activity, BBB traversal, and immune reprogramming observed in rodent glioma models have driven the initiation of a growing number of early-phase clinical trials. These studies leveraged multiple translational advantages. The use of 5-ALA enabled the repurpose of a clinically familiar compound as a sonosensitizer, streamlining toxicology requirements. In parallel, recent advances in helmet-based LIFU technology allowed safe and precise delivery of acoustic energy through the intact human skull under MRI or neuronavigational guidance, making the intervention fully outpatient and repeatable.

Importantly, the inclusion of correlative imaging and biopsy endpoints, such as PpIX fluorescence, intraoperative ROS adduct detection, diffusion-weighted MRI, and caspase-3 immunostaining, provided a means to confirm on-target biological effects and adjust sonication parameters in real time. Across trials, design variables have spanned a range of sensitizer regimens, ultrasound schedules, and therapeutic settings, including recurrent GBM, perioperative resection, and combination with chemoradiation or immunotherapy. Safety outcomes to date have been favorable, with no dose-limiting toxicities, no device-related grade ≥3 adverse events, and overall procedural tolerability compatible with outpatient workflows. Early efficacy signals, including extension of median overall survival to approximately 16 months in heavily pretreated GBM, partial radiographic responses in diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, and biopsy-confirmed oxidative damage, support the continued clinical exploration of SDT. sec.title: CHALLENGES AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
sec.p: SDT for GBM still has a number of obstacles to overcome before it can be completely incorporated into clinical practice, despite promising outcomes in preclinical and early clinical research [65]. The inherent complexity of transferring SDT from concept to practical implementation is reflected in these difficulties, which cut across technical, pharmacological, biological, and regulatory domains [66]. The standardization and optimization of sonication parameters is one of the main technical obstacles. Variables like frequency, intensity, duty cycle, burst duration, and timing in relation to sensitizer administration have a significant impact on SDT efficacy. These parameters, however, vary greatly between studies and are frequently customized for tumor models or devices. To guarantee consistency and reproducibility as the field moves closer to multi-center clinical trials, harmonized protocols and real-time dosimetry tools will be crucial. The creation of clinically scalable sensitizers and nanomedicine platforms presents similar difficulties [67]. Next-generation formulations like oxygen-generating nanoparticles, biomimetic carriers, and piezoelectric constructs are still in the early stages of development, despite the viability of agents like 5-ALA. These systems need to strike a balance between long-term stability, safety in both systemic and intracranial settings, tumor selectivity, and ROS-generating potency [68]. Oral administration further increases complexity, which calls for strong resistance to gastrointestinal breakdown, effective mucosal absorption, and low first-pass metabolism [69].

Another significant obstacle is heterogeneity in the integrity of the BBB. The spatial and temporal dynamics of this process are still not fully understood, although ultrasound can temporarily increase BBB permeability [70]. Furthermore, there may be dangers associated with frequent or extensive BBB disruption, such as neuroinflammation or off-target effects. Accurate acoustic targeting, real-time imaging, and the incorporation of receptor-targeted nanomedicines are likely to be necessary for safe and successful approaches [71]. The SDT response is made more difficult by biological heterogeneity. The degree of immune activation and susceptibility to ROS-mediated cytotoxicity can be impacted by inter-patient variations in tumor genotype, metabolism, and immune profile. For example, tumors with hypoxia or increased antioxidant capacity may be able to withstand ROS insult, whereas immunosuppressive myeloid cells may reduce immunogenic responses. Using imaging, ctDNA, or functional sonobiopsy, biomarker-guided stratification could determine which patients are most likely to benefit.

Clinically speaking, adding SDT to current treatment paradigms raises new therapeutic and logistical issues [72]. SDT can be used as a maintenance strategy after chemoradiation, as a neoadjuvant to sterilize tumor margins, or in conjunction with immunotherapy to improve immune priming [25]. Sensitizer administration, sonication timing, and patient adherence will all need to be carefully coordinated for each of these strategies, particularly when using outpatient, multi-session protocols. SDT complicates approval processes because it falls into a hybrid category between drugs, devices, and biologics. Ultrasound systems are governed by class II or III medical device regulations, whereas sensitizers may be evaluated as medications or combination products. It will be crucial to have clear regulatory guidance, particularly when it comes to the combination of oncology products [73]. To reduce risk of wider clinical use, strong safety datasets in both adult and pediatric populations will be required concurrently.

Looking forward, several opportunities are poised to advance the field. Theragnostic SDT platforms that combine real-time imaging and ultrasound activation may enable feedback-controlled therapy and adaptive treatment planning. The incorporation of artificial intelligence for treatment, optimization, and prediction may enhance both precision and scalability. Synergistic combinations with checkpoint inhibitors, metabolic reprogramming agents, or ferroptosis inducers may expand the therapeutic envelope. In summary, while significant barriers to translation persist, SDT integrates tumor biology, nanomedicine, and ultrasound physics in a way that could establish it as a non-invasive, image-guided, and safe therapeutic modality. SDT has the potential to significantly improve the treatment of one of the most difficult cancers in neuro-oncology with continued interdisciplinary cooperation.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: SDT represents a compelling frontier in the treatment of GBM, offering a novel convergence of focused ultrasound physics, redox-based cytotoxicity, and nanoparticle-enabled drug delivery. Its ability to bypass traditional barriers such as the BBB, deliver spatially confined cytotoxic effects, and induce tumor-specific immune responses positions SDT as a unique and potentially transformative modality. The development of orally administered, ultrasound-responsive nanomedicines further expands the translational scope of SDT, enabling repeatable, outpatient-compatible treatments for patients with inoperable or recurrent GBM. While challenges remain, ranging from standardization of sonication protocols to regulatory alignment for drug-device combination products, the rapid pace of preclinical innovation and early clinical success suggests that SDT may soon transition from experimental concept to clinical reality. With sustained interdisciplinary collaboration, SDT has the potential to redefine therapeutic boundaries in neuro-oncology and offer new hope for patients facing this devastating disease.
